payload.proof_nl:
Let S be a numerical semigroup as in the statement, and let m be its multiplicity, i.e. the least positive element of S, with m >= 2. For each r with 1 <= r <= m-1, let w_r be the least element of S congruent to r modulo m, and write
w_r = r + m k_r.
We first justify that each k_r is a positive integer. Since w_r ≡ r (mod m), the quotient k_r = (w_r-r)/m is an integer. Also w_r cannot equal r, because 1 <= r <= m-1 and m is the least positive element of S, so no positive integer smaller than m belongs to S. Hence w_r > r, so k_r >= 1.

Now fix integers i,j with 1 <= i <= j <= m-1.
Because w_i,w_j are in S and S is closed under addition, w_i + w_j belongs to S.
We consider the two cases from the statement.

Case 1: i + j < m.
Then
w_i + w_j = (i + m k_i) + (j + m k_j) = (i+j) + m(k_i+k_j).
So w_i+w_j is an element of S congruent to i+j modulo m. Since 1 <= i+j <= m-1, the residue class i+j is one of the classes for which w_{i+j} is defined, and by definition w_{i+j} is the least element of S congruent to i+j modulo m. Therefore
w_{i+j} <= w_i + w_j.
Substituting the expressions for these numbers gives
(i+j) + m k_{i+j} <= (i+j) + m(k_i+k_j).
Subtract i+j from both sides:
m k_{i+j} <= m(k_i+k_j).
Since m > 0, divide by m to obtain
k_{i+j} <= k_i + k_j,
that is,
k_i + k_j >= k_{i+j}.
This is exactly the first Kunz inequality.

Case 2: i + j > m.
Then 1 <= i+j-m <= m-2 < m, so the index i+j-m lies in {1,...,m-1}, and w_{i+j-m} is defined. Again,
w_i + w_j = (i + m k_i) + (j + m k_j) = (i+j-m) + m(k_i+k_j+1).
Hence w_i+w_j is an element of S congruent to i+j-m modulo m. Since w_{i+j-m} is the least element of S in that congruence class, we have
w_{i+j-m} <= w_i + w_j.
Substituting the expressions gives
(i+j-m) + m k_{i+j-m} <= (i+j-m) + m(k_i+k_j+1).
Subtract i+j-m from both sides:
m k_{i+j-m} <= m(k_i+k_j+1).
Since m > 0, divide by m to obtain
k_{i+j-m} <= k_i + k_j + 1,
that is,
k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_{i+j-m}.
This is exactly the second Kunz inequality.

Since the two required implications have been proved for every 1 <= i <= j <= m-1, the tuple (k_1,...,k_{m-1}) satisfies the stated Kunz inequalities. This proves the lemma.
payload.role_in_assembly: Shows that every numerical semigroup counted by N(m,g) determines an admissible Kunz vector.

domain_restrictions: m is an integer with m >= 2
g is an integer with g >= 0
g+1 is therefore an integer >= 1 (so genus value g+1 is within the stated integer domain)
root_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all integers m >= 2 and all integers g >= 0, the counting function N(m,g) is monotonically nondecreasing in g with step size 1: N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1).

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For any numerical semigroup S ⊆ N0 with 0∈S, additively closed, and with finite complement in N0, let m be its multiplicity (least positive element) with m≥2. For each residue r with 1≤r≤m−1, let w_r be the least element of S such that w_r≡r (mod m), and write w_r=r+m k_r with k_r∈Z_{>0}. Then for all integers i,j with 1≤i≤j≤m−1: (i+j<m ⇒ k_i+k_j≥k_{i+j}) and (i+j>m ⇒ k_i+k_j+1≥k_{i+j−m}). No condition is specified for i+j=m.

∀ r ∈ Z with 1 ≤ r ≤ m-1, ∃ w_r (least element) in S such that w_r ≡ r (mod m)
∀ i,j ∈ Z with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ m-1, (two-branch conditions on i+j relative to m) apply to k_i,k_j,k_{...}

payload.statement_nl: Let S be a subset of N0 = {0,1,2,...} such that 0 belongs to S, S is closed under addition, and N0 \ S is finite; in other words, S is a numerical semigroup. Let m be the least positive element of S, and assume m >= 2. For each integer r with 1 <= r <= m-1, let w_r be the least element of S congruent to r modulo m, and write w_r = r + m k_r with k_r a positive integer. Then the tuple (k_1, ..., k_{m-1}) satisfies the Kunz inequalities: for all integers i and j with 1 <= i <= j <= m-1, if i + j < m then k_i + k_j >= k_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_{i+j-m}.

detailed_findings.finding: The proof correctly shows k_r is an integer and strictly positive from w_r > r and the fact that no positive integer less than m lies in S.
In the case i+j<m, the proof validly uses that w_i+w_j is in S and has residue i+j mod m, so minimality of w_{i+j} gives the desired inequality.
In the case i+j>m, the rewritten decomposition of w_i+w_j as (i+j-m)+m(k_i+k_j+1) is correct, and the range check for i+j-m ensures the target index is defined.
The proof respects the semantic sketch and correctly leaves out the boundary case i+j=m, for which no Kunz inequality is claimed here.

result_payload.reason: The proof correctly derives the two Kunz inequalities from the minimality of the Apéry representatives w_r and additive closure of the numerical semigroup. The positivity of each k_r is justified using the multiplicity property m = min(S \ {0}). Both index-range checks are handled properly for the cases i+j<m and i+j>m, and the boundary case i+j=m is correctly omitted because the statement imposes no condition there. The argument matches the lemma sketch and supports the root theorem role by showing any numerical semigroup yields an admissible Kunz vector.
